title: Is Smile 2 a Success or a Failure as a Sequel?

commenti.body: This one wasn’t about grief. It was about agency. Skye Riley has no control over her life. All of her decisions are made for her by her mother, choreographer, entourage, etc.  When she does try to take control and succeeds - like when she grabs the steering wheel - bad things happen.

I pretty much sure your attitude toward the original film so I'm not really in the market to see this while it's still in the theaters. "Grief horror" (if that's a term) is essentially just a subset of "psychological horror" to begin with, where it's easy to get lazy simply because an essential part of the premise is whether these events are actually occurring or are all in the character's head. Few such movies really strike a good balance IMO. "Smile" certainly wasn't the worst horror movie I've ever seen but it's way to "meh" to celebrate as a proper triumph of the genre IMO.

I liked it, but I didn't think it was better than the original like a lot of people. I was interested in following Kyle Gallner's character because he already had an idea of what was going on from the first film. The first scene was the best part of the movie and then after that it goes through the same beats as the first film with a different character, but even worse we find out at the end that most of what we just saw didn't happen anyway.

What you're saying is that Smile 2 is not the movie you want it to be, and you're judging it by the standard of another movie that exists in your mind, if you do this every movie is bad

Judge it by the movie that it is, then you can start creating an actual judgment, you didn't like the first movie -which was a great success by all accounts- and somehow think the movie should be something different... why? So does it appeal to you? 

You're so focused in grief that you didn't even notice that the movie talks about agency, the monster is something that takes your agency away (like addiction, controlling parents, fame, etc), the first one follows a main character (psychologist) that deals with the scars of psychological trauma, this one deals with a main character that isn't trying to figure what the monster is, just want to gain control of her life because she lost it, long before the monster took possession of her

>Personally, I'm also getting very tired of grief horror (especially horror where the monster is a stand in for grief or trauma).

But it's not a bout grief at all. The monster is very bluntly a metaphor for drug addiction, and the protagonist's addiction seems to ve largely driven by her lack of agency in her life, as another poster explained already. 

She doesn't even grieve on screen for her jerkass boyfriend, like at all. 

>Sam Raimi did essentially remake the original Evil Dead film, but he also expanded on the lore and added new story elements that made it clear the film was acting both as a redux and a sequel.

Lore is a concept from geek and gaming communities that is ingrained in story telling conventions and tropes from their chosen medium (long running, franchise driven and engagement based). 

I don't think this film has any particular interest in doing world building or anything like that. It's not even particularly interested in telling a story. It's a character study first ad foremost.
